title: Memory supports for appointment attendance
stem: A client recovering from psychosis understands the purpose and dates of appointments but forgets them during the week. They manage a smartphone independently, check the noticeboard beside their keys daily and want to attend independently. Which additions most directly compensate for the reported memory difficulty? Select all that apply.
options: Enter agreed reminders in the phone calendar
Repeat a longer explanation of the service at each visit
Place a clear appointment cue beside the keys
Ask a relative to book the appointments for the client
Provide a detailed leaflet about the benefits of follow-up
why: Time-linked prompts use a tool the client already manages to cue the intended action.
The purpose is already understood; additional explanation does not directly provide a cue when the appointment is approaching.
A visible reminder at an established daily stopping point links the information to an existing routine.
Changing who books the visit does not address remembering the agreed date during the week.
More information about benefits does not directly compensate for the described prospective-memory difficulty.
takeaway: Match practical environmental prompts to the specific cognitive difficulty and the client's established routines.
learningObjective: Match practical environmental prompts to the specific cognitive difficulty and the client's established routines.

title: Naloxone follow-up teaching
stem: A client's family learns to use take-home naloxone. Which additional message is essential?
options: Recovery after naloxone means emergency assessment is unnecessary
Naloxone permanently removes all opioid effects
Call emergency help and continue monitoring because effects can recur
Save naloxone only for people with a confirmed prescription
why: Initial improvement may be temporary.
Naloxone's effect may wear off before the opioid's effect.
Emergency response and ongoing observation remain necessary after administration.
Suspected opioid poisoning warrants response regardless of prescription status.
takeaway: Teach that naloxone reversal is temporary and does not replace emergency care.
learningObjective: Teach that naloxone reversal is temporary and does not replace emergency care.

title: Lower tolerance after abstinence
stem: A client leaving treatment asks about returning to a previous opioid amount after weeks without use. What should the nurse explain?
options: Reduced tolerance can increase overdose risk; discuss prevention and treatment supports
The previously tolerated amount remains equally safe
Only the source of the opioid changes risk
Tolerance always returns before harmful effects occur
why: Abstinence can reduce tolerance, making recurrence particularly hazardous.
Past tolerance does not establish present safety.
Dose, tolerance, combinations and supply can all affect risk.
There is no assurance tolerance returns before toxicity.
takeaway: Discuss increased overdose risk after reduced opioid exposure.
learningObjective: Discuss increased overdose risk after reduced opioid exposure.

title: Mixed-drug overdose concern
stem: A family asks whether to withhold naloxone if an unresponsive person's substance exposure is uncertain. What should teaching emphasize?
options: Wait for proof of an opioid before calling help
Use naloxone instead of contacting emergency services
Assume naloxone reverses every sedating substance
Follow emergency response guidance and use naloxone when opioid poisoning is suspected
why: Waiting can delay lifesaving response.
Naloxone does not replace emergency care and supportive measures.
Nonopioid effects may persist even when opioids are reversed.
Suspected opioid involvement warrants prompt response despite incomplete information.
takeaway: Respond to suspected opioid poisoning without waiting for certainty.
learningObjective: Respond to suspected opioid poisoning without waiting for certainty.

title: Preparing an overdose prevention plan
stem: Which topics should be included when a client may return to nonprescribed opioid use? Select all that apply.
options: Access to naloxone and knowing how to use it
Lower tolerance after a period without use
Assuming familiar packaging guarantees drug contents
Available local overdose-prevention and treatment services
Avoiding discussion unless the client promises abstinence
why: Ready access and training support a timely response.
Tolerance changes are an important overdose risk.
Appearance or packaging cannot establish contents or potency.
Local services can provide prevention and treatment support.
Harm-reduction discussion should not depend on an abstinence promise.
takeaway: Provide practical overdose prevention alongside treatment options.
learningObjective: Provide practical overdose prevention alongside treatment options.

title: Opioid withdrawal distress
stem: A client with opioid dependence develops yawning, diffuse aches, diarrhea and restlessness after interruption of use. What is the best response?
options: Treat distress as misconduct before assessment
Assess withdrawal, hydration and treatment needs without judgment
Assume every symptom is an overdose
Require counselling participation before addressing physical symptoms
why: Behavioural blame can delay needed physical care.
Symptom assessment supports appropriate treatment and engagement.
Withdrawal and overdose patterns differ and require assessment.
Physical needs should not be conditional on counselling participation.
takeaway: Assess opioid withdrawal symptoms and physical needs promptly.
learningObjective: Assess opioid withdrawal symptoms and physical needs promptly.

title: Stimulant-related acute symptoms
stem: A client reports recent stimulant use and now has chest pain, severe agitation and overheating. What is the priority?
options: Begin a detailed relapse-prevention interview
Encourage vigorous movement to release tension
Arrange emergency physical assessment and maintain a safe low-stimulation setting
Wait for sleep to resolve the symptoms
why: Counselling is secondary to possible acute medical toxicity.
Exertion may worsen overheating and cardiovascular strain.
These symptoms can signal serious toxicity requiring urgent care.
Waiting risks deterioration from potentially life-threatening complications.
takeaway: Escalate cardiovascular and heat-related symptoms after stimulant use.
learningObjective: Escalate cardiovascular and heat-related symptoms after stimulant use.

title: Cannabis-related anxiety
stem: A client develops marked anxiety and suspiciousness after a high-potency cannabis product. What should the nurse do?
options: Assess exposure, physical status and safety in a calm setting
Assume legalization means the symptoms are unrelated
Debate every suspicious statement before assessment
Recommend another dose to establish tolerance
why: Assessment addresses intoxication, possible complications and immediate support needs.
Legal availability does not eliminate adverse effects.
Argument can worsen distress and delay evaluation.
Additional exposure may intensify symptoms.
takeaway: Assess acute mental and physical changes after cannabis exposure.
learningObjective: Assess acute mental and physical changes after cannabis exposure.

title: Concurrent mental-health and substance needs
stem: A client with depression drinks to manage distress and is told to address only one condition first. What plan is more appropriate?
options: Defer all mood care until permanent abstinence
Defer all alcohol assessment until mood completely resolves
Refer separately without communication between services
Coordinate assessment and support for both interacting concerns
why: Delaying mood care may leave a driver of distress untreated.
Alcohol-related risks need assessment even while depression is treated.
Fragmentation may miss interactions and create conflicting plans.
Integrated care addresses the overlapping clinical and practical needs.
takeaway: Coordinate care for co-occurring mental-health and substance-use conditions.
learningObjective: Coordinate care for co-occurring mental-health and substance-use conditions.

title: Evaluating recovery support
stem: Which outcomes indicate useful progress in a client's substance-use recovery plan? Select all that apply.
options: Earlier help-seeking when cravings increase
Improved participation in valued daily roles
Willingness to agree with every staff opinion
Reduced harmful use patterns according to the agreed goals
Avoiding appointments to prevent embarrassment
why: Timely help-seeking demonstrates use of support before escalation.
Recovery includes meaningful functioning and participation.
Agreement alone does not establish clinical progress.
Outcomes should reflect the collaboratively defined harm and use targets.
Missed care may reduce support during difficulties.
takeaway: Evaluate recovery through agreed goals, functioning and use of support.
learningObjective: Evaluate recovery through agreed goals, functioning and use of support.

title: Gambling-related financial distress
stem: A client reports chasing gambling losses and hiding debt from family. What should the nurse assess first?
options: Preferred game and expected winning strategy
Immediate safety, financial harm, control over gambling and available supports
Whether the client can win enough to repay the debt
Only the family's opinion of gambling
why: Game preference alone does not assess harm or urgency.
Gambling-related distress can include serious financial and suicide risks.
Further gambling may increase rather than resolve harm.
The client's pattern and safety need direct assessment.
takeaway: Assess safety and functional harm in problematic gambling.
learningObjective: Assess safety and functional harm in problematic gambling.

title: Problematic gaming and function
stem: A student games late into the night and repeatedly misses classes but denies any difficulty. What should the nurse explore?
options: Whether the game is currently popular
Whether parents dislike technology
Sleep, control over use, missed responsibilities and the student's goals
Whether the device is expensive
why: Popularity does not determine functional impact.
Family attitudes do not replace assessment of the student's experience.
Function and control distinguish a preferred activity from a harmful pattern.
Price does not establish severity or support needs.
takeaway: Assess control and functional impairment in potentially addictive behaviours.
learningObjective: Assess control and functional impairment in potentially addictive behaviours.

title: Family boundaries during recovery
stem: A parent asks whether paying every gambling debt will protect their adult child. What should the nurse do?
options: Explore boundaries and support options without taking over family decisions
Instruct the parent to pay all debts immediately
Recommend ending every relationship with the client
Focus only on the interest rate of the debt
why: Collaborative discussion can address support, safety and enabling patterns.
Automatic payment may not address the underlying harmful behaviour.
Complete cutoff is not a universal therapeutic requirement.
Financial details alone miss the family and behavioural issues.
takeaway: Help families distinguish supportive involvement from taking over consequences.
learningObjective: Help families distinguish supportive involvement from taking over consequences.

title: Choosing peer support
stem: A client wants recovery support but felt uncomfortable in a previous group. What is the best response?
options: Insist that one group is the only effective option
Interpret discomfort as proof of low motivation
Stop discussing peer support entirely
Explore what did not fit and offer suitable alternatives
why: Recovery supports differ in approach and fit.
Discomfort may reflect format, accessibility or preference.
One poor fit does not exclude all peer support.
Tailored alternatives support informed engagement.
takeaway: Match recovery supports to the client's needs and preferences.
learningObjective: Match recovery supports to the client's needs and preferences.

title: Planning after a substance-related admission
stem: Which discharge details require clarification for a client entering community treatment? Select all that apply.
options: How the first appointment will be reached
Who will address urgent withdrawal or recurrence concerns
Whether a referral name alone proves treatment has started
How prescribed treatment will continue without an access gap
Whether the client can promise never to have cravings
why: Transport and access determine whether follow-up is feasible.
Clear urgent contacts support timely response to deterioration.
Referral issuance does not confirm connection to care.
Treatment continuity can prevent avoidable destabilization.
Cravings cannot be eliminated by a promise.
takeaway: Confirm operational follow-up and treatment continuity after admission.
learningObjective: Confirm operational follow-up and treatment continuity after admission.

title: Strengths in mental-health recovery
stem: A client says the only meaningful goal is returning to caring for a garden. Which plan best reflects recovery-oriented care?
options: Replace the goal with a standard ward target
Link treatment and supports to gradual return to gardening
Require complete symptom absence before discussing it
Use staff convenience to decide the final goal
why: Standard targets may miss the client's motivation and values.
A valued role can organize meaningful recovery steps.
Participation can improve before every symptom disappears.
Service routines should not define the client's personal recovery.
takeaway: Organize recovery goals around what the client finds meaningful.
learningObjective: Organize recovery goals around what the client finds meaningful.

title: Supported employment goal
stem: A client recovering from severe mental illness wants to work but fears disclosing the diagnosis. What should the nurse do?
options: Tell the client to disclose to every coworker
Discourage employment until confidence is perfect
Explore goals and connect with appropriate vocational and disclosure advice
Choose the employer without involving the client
why: Disclosure decisions are individualized and involve privacy considerations.
Supported work planning need not wait for perfect confidence.
Specialist support can address function, accommodations and informed choice.
The client's preferences and participation are central.
takeaway: Support employment goals with individualized practical and privacy advice.
learningObjective: Support employment goals with individualized practical and privacy advice.

title: Self-stigma after diagnosis
stem: A client says, 'Having a mental illness means I cannot be a good parent.' What response is best?
options: Explore the concern and identify parenting strengths and support needs
Agree that diagnosis determines parenting ability
Offer reassurance without discussing actual functioning
Ask relatives to judge the client's worth as a parent
why: Function, strengths and needed support are more informative than a label.
Diagnosis alone does not determine parenting capacity.
Unsupported reassurance may miss real concerns or helpful resources.
Worth judgments do not provide a clinical assessment.
takeaway: Challenge self-stigma through individualized strengths and functional assessment.
learningObjective: Challenge self-stigma through individualized strengths and functional assessment.

title: Shared decisions in recovery
stem: A client finds the current treatment plan burdensome and wants changes. They are stable and capable of participating. What should the nurse do?
options: Explain that stability removes the need to discuss concerns
Change all treatments independently
Ask family to overrule the client's preferences
Clarify burdens and goals and arrange collaborative treatment review
why: Burden can affect sustainability even when symptoms are stable.
Changes require appropriate authority and clinical coordination.
Family preference does not replace capable participation.
Shared review balances preferences, benefits, risks and feasible options.
takeaway: Include treatment burden in collaborative recovery planning.
learningObjective: Include treatment burden in collaborative recovery planning.

title: Measuring community recovery
stem: Which indicators can help evaluate a community mental-health plan? Select all that apply.
options: Progress toward the client's chosen housing or activity goals
Access to support when early difficulties appear
Absence of any disagreement with clinicians
The client's sense of choice and participation
Number of pamphlets provided as the sole outcome
why: Personal goals reflect meaningful life outcomes.
Usable support can prevent avoidable crises.
Agreement does not establish recovery or quality of care.
Agency is an important recovery-oriented outcome.
Materials distributed do not demonstrate benefit.
takeaway: Evaluate recovery using function, access and client-defined participation.
learningObjective: Evaluate recovery using function, access and client-defined participation.

title: Grief around an anniversary
stem: A client functioning well after a partner's death becomes tearful near the anniversary. What is the best response?
options: Reassess supports and discuss what this date means to the client
Conclude the earlier recovery was not real
Advise cancelling every remembrance activity
Focus on how many months grief should last
why: Anniversary reactions can renew grief and benefit from individualized support.
Renewed emotion does not erase previous adaptation.
Remembrance preferences differ and should be explored.
A fixed timetable does not describe an individual's grief.
takeaway: Explore anniversary-related grief in the context of meaning and function.
learningObjective: Explore anniversary-related grief in the context of meaning and function.

title: Anticipatory grief
stem: A spouse caring for a terminally ill partner says, 'I already miss our old life, even though they are alive.' What should the nurse say?
options: 'Focus on being grateful they are still here.'
'You are grieving changes and losses that are happening now.'
'Save these feelings for after the death.'
'This means you are ready to stop caring for them.'
why: Gratitude framing can suppress valid feelings of loss.
Anticipatory grief can occur before death and include current changes.
Emotional support is appropriate before as well as after death.
Grief does not establish a wish to abandon caregiving.
takeaway: Recognize grief for losses occurring before an anticipated death.
learningObjective: Recognize grief for losses occurring before an anticipated death.

title: Grieving different ways
stem: After a child's death, one parent wants to talk and the other prefers quiet activity. Both remain engaged in daily life. What should the nurse emphasize?
options: The quieter parent is necessarily avoiding grief
Both parents should use identical coping methods
Different expressions can be valid; explore how each wants support
The more tearful parent has the more serious loss
why: Quiet coping does not by itself establish pathological avoidance.
Grief expression differs among individuals.
Mutual understanding can support both people without ranking responses.
Visible emotion does not measure the importance of the loss.
takeaway: Support different grief expressions without ranking their validity.
learningObjective: Support different grief expressions without ranking their validity.

title: A child asks about death
stem: A young child asks why a deceased grandparent will not wake up. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Say the grandparent is sleeping deeply
Explain the entire organ-failure sequence
Change the topic to protect the child
Use simple direct language that the body stopped working and cannot wake
why: Sleep language can confuse death with normal sleep.
Technical detail may exceed the child's developmental needs.
Avoidance leaves the child's question and possible fears unresolved.
Concrete honest language supports understanding without confusing euphemisms.
takeaway: Explain death to children using clear developmentally appropriate language.
learningObjective: Explain death to children using clear developmentally appropriate language.

title: Grief requiring further assessment
stem: Which findings in a bereaved client warrant additional clinical assessment? Select all that apply.
options: Persistent inability to meet basic needs
Suicidal thoughts with intent
Occasional tears while discussing memories
Marked sustained functional deterioration
Choosing a culturally meaningful mourning practice
why: Basic self-care failure can create immediate health needs.
Intent requires prompt safety assessment.
Tearfulness alone can occur during adaptive grieving.
Sustained impairment may require additional support or treatment.
Cultural practices should not be pathologized without context.
takeaway: Assess safety and sustained impairment rather than judging grief by tears alone.
learningObjective: Assess safety and sustained impairment rather than judging grief by tears alone.

title: An unrecognized loss
stem: A client grieves the death of a former partner, but relatives say the relationship should no longer matter. What is the best nursing response?
options: Focus only on relatives with current legal relationships
Acknowledge the client's loss and ask what support would help
Advise avoiding mention of the relationship
Determine whether the family approves before offering support
why: Emotional significance is not determined solely by formal relationship status.
Recognizing the loss supports someone whose grief is socially minimized.
Silence may deepen isolation.
Family approval is not required to acknowledge distress.
takeaway: Recognize grief even when others do not validate the relationship or loss.
learningObjective: Recognize grief even when others do not validate the relationship or loss.
